name: Context Engineering 2.0: The Context of Context Engineering (arXiv:2510.26493)
publisher: GAIR-NLP / SII research group (Qishuo Hua, Lyumanshan Ye, Dayuan Fu, Yang Xiao, Xiaojie Cai, Yunze Wu, Jifan Lin, Junfei Wang, Pengfei Liu); arXiv preprint
claim_value: Context engineering is not a product of the 2023-2025 agent/LLM boom but a practice with over 20 years of history, which the paper periodizes into four eras: Era 1.0 (1990s-2020, 'Primitive Computation', rigid structured-input HCI/ubiquitous-computing systems), Era 2.0 (2020-present, 'Agent-Centric Intelligence', LLM-driven agents handling prompt engineering, RAG, tool calling, and long-term memory), Era 3.0 (future, 'Human-Level Intelligence', nuanced reasoning over ambiguous context), and Era 4.0 (speculative, 'Superhuman Intelligence', systems that construct context for humans rather than the reverse). It defines context engineering as an entropy-reduction process converting high-entropy, ambiguous human context into low-entropy, machine-interpretable representations, and proposes design principles ('Minimal Sufficiency', 'Semantic Continuity') meant to apply across the whole pipeline (collection, storage, representation, multimodal fusion, abstraction/'self-baking', selection, dynamic adaptation).
claim_definition: This is a conceptual/theoretical framework and historical survey, not a benchmark or empirical study. It asserts a taxonomy (the four eras) and a formal framing (entropy reduction, set-theoretic/functional composition of context operations) rather than measuring anything. Prompt engineering and RAG are explicitly treated as techniques subordinate to context engineering, not as separate or competing terms.
evidence_category: survey opinion / conceptual framework (no benchmark or empirical result)
reproducibility: Not applicable: paper has no code-dependent empirical claims. It does provide a public GitHub repo (github.com/GAIR-NLP/Context-Engineering-2.0) and companion site (context.opensii.ai) with supplementary material, but these support the conceptual framework/taxonomy rather than a reproducible experiment.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: no - GAIR-NLP is an academic research lab (affiliated with Shanghai Innovation Institute / SII per the companion site 'opensii.ai'); authors are researchers, not a vendor with a context/memory/vector-DB product to promote. [uncertain on exact institutional affiliation details]
conflict_notes: No specific figure-level discrepancy found versus how this paper is cited elsewhere (it is too recent, Oct 2026 submission, to have accumulated secondary citations with numeric claims). The paper itself flags its own gaps: the entropy-reduction framing has no quantified metric tying it to task performance, the four-era transitions have no operational/empirical criteria, and 'Minimal Sufficiency'/'Semantic Continuity' are asserted conceptually without algorithms or measurable constraints - i.e., the paper's own stated limitations undercut how 'rigorous' a reader might otherwise take the discipline claim to be.
relationship: Complicates the 'prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is what matters now' framing from a different angle than most industry sources: rather than disputing whether prompt engineering still matters, it denies that context engineering is a new or 2025-coined idea at all, arguing it has been continuously practiced for 20+ years and that prompt engineering/RAG/tool calling/memory are just techniques nested inside it. This reframes the whole debate as a terminology/periodization dispute rather than a question of which skill is obsolete.
derivative_of: Explicitly extends Mei et al., 'A Survey of Context Engineering for Large Language Models' (arXiv:2507.13334), which the authors say was LLM-practice-focused; this paper broadens that into a longer historical trajectory (HCI/ubiquitous computing through agentic LLMs) and adds a formal (set-theoretic/entropy) framing. It cites Anthropic, LangChain, AutoGPT, and Letta as examples of 'Era 2.0' implementations of principles the authors say predate them, effectively positioning current industry blog-post framings (Anthropic's, LangChain's) as instances of an older pattern rather than original insights.
register: academic researcher, with secondary relevance to practitioner/engineer readers (via its taxonomy of techniques); not pitched at enterprise IT buyers.
confidence: secondary_unverified - full PDF text could not be reliably extracted directly (compressed/non-machine-readable text layer); findings are built from the arXiv HTML rendering, the paper's own abstract, and a third-party summary (emergentmind.com). Core structural claims (four eras, entropy framing, Mei et al. as predecessor, no empirical content) were corroborated across two independent fetches, but direct quotation accuracy from the primary PDF is unverified. [uncertain]
notes: Two independent extraction attempts (arXiv HTML render and a third-party summarizer) agreed on the four-era structure, the entropy-reduction definition, and the paper's self-identified lack of empirical validation, which gives reasonable confidence in those points. No numeric/statistical claim exists in this source to cross-check against secondary citations elsewhere.

new_angle: Adds an academic, non-vendor voice arguing the 'context engineering' label itself is not novel terminology from the 2025 agent boom but a 20+ year old practice, which is a different and sharper version of the 'rebrand' critique than most blog-level commentary offers: it doesn't just say 'this is just RAG with a new name,' it historicizes the whole lineage back to 1990s HCI and offers a four-era taxonomy plus an explicit, self-acknowledged lack of empirical grounding (no metrics, no benchmarks, no transition criteria) for the 'discipline' it proposes. Useful as the strongest 'this is old wine' counterpoint available from inside academia rather than from a competing vendor or blogger.
